meta.title: Who really said "It puts the lotion on its skin, or else it gets the hose again"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Nobody. The actual line is "It rubs the lotion on its skin" — written by Ted Tally for The Silence of the Lambs (1991). "Puts" comes from the basket line.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It puts the lotion on its skin, or else it gets the hose again'?
meta.ogDescription: It's "rubs," not "puts." Ted Tally wrote the line for the 1991 film — and the scene itself comes from Thomas Harris's 1988 novel.

answer.label: Not quite — the actual line is “It rubs the lotion on its skin”
answer.authorDates: b. 1952 · wrote the screenplay for The Silence of the Lambs (1991)
answer.sourceLine: In Jonathan Demme’s The Silence of the Lambs (1991), Jame “Buffalo Bill” Gumb says “It rubs the lotion on its skin, or else it gets the hose again” — rubs, never puts. The scene and the hose threat come from Thomas Harris’s 1988 novel, but the dehumanising third-person sentence people quote is screenwriter Ted Tally’s; the popular “puts” is borrowed from the next line, where Gumb tells her to place the lotion in the basket.

source.heading: What was actually said

source.excerpt: It rubs the lotion on its skin. It does this whenever it’s told. … It rubs the lotion on its skin, or else it gets the hose again.
trail: The wording. Wikiquote’s transcription ↗ gives the line as “It rubs the lotion on its skin, or else it gets the hose again”, and the shooting script posted at IMSDb ↗ agrees. Both read rubs; neither contains “puts the lotion on its skin”.

The origin. The scene is not the film’s invention: Thomas Harris’s novel ↗ (St. Martin’s Press, 1988) already has the pit, the floodlamp, the threatened hose and a bottle of skin emollient. Reading that passage, two differences stand out: Harris’s Gumb addresses Catherine as you (“or you’ll get the hose”; “rub the cream all over”), and the word lotion never appears in the scene at all.

The pronoun. Tally’s drafts at the Internet Archive ↗ show the change happening. The drafts of 28 July and 25 August 1989 keep Harris’s second person — “Rub it in! Or you’ll get the hose again” — using “it” only in the aside to the dog. In the 15 January 1990 draft the third-person construction has taken over the commands themselves.

The credit. Wikipedia ↗ records Ted Tally as sole screenwriter and winner of the Best Adapted Screenplay Oscar at the 64th Academy Awards; the film was distributed by Orion Pictures and released 14 February 1991.
source.cutTag: Gumb, at the mouth of the oubliette
source.excerptNote: The verb is rubs. “Puts” does occur in the scene — but in Gumb’s next instruction, transcribed by Wikiquote as “Now it places the lotion in the basket”, and in the shouted “Put the fucking lotion in the basket!” The popular quote welds the famous sentence to the shouted verb.

source.rightsNote: This is a 1991 screen line, so it is firmly in copyright — US public domain currently reaches only works published through 1930. Screenwriting is work-for-hire, so the copyright sits with the studio rather than with Ted Tally personally: the film was produced by Strong Heart Productions and distributed by Orion Pictures ↗, whose post-1982 library passed to MGM after its 1997 sale and is now held under Amazon MGM Studios. The underlying novel (1988) remains separately in copyright to Thomas Harris and St. Martin’s Press.

author.name: Ted Tally
author.heading: Who actually wrote the line
author.bio: Ted Tally (William Theodore Tally, born 9 April 1952) is an American playwright and screenwriter who came to film from the theatre, where his play Terra Nova won an Obie Award. His adaptation of Thomas Harris’s novel The Silence of the Lambs won him the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay at the 64th Academy Awards, along with the Writers Guild and Edgar awards. He later adapted Red Dragon (2002) and All the Pretty Horses, but declined to write Hannibal.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited here — the film is real, the scene is real, and the line is nearly real. Three things drift: one verb, one author, and the difference between a writer and the man on screen.

items.why: The verb is rubs. Wikiquote’s transcription ↗ gives “It rubs the lotion on its skin, or else it gets the hose again”, and Tally’s screenplay ↗ reads the same. “Puts” is imported from Gumb’s next instruction, about placing the lotion in the basket.

Goodreads files the line under “Thomas Harris, The Silence of the Lambs” ↗, as if it were the novel’s prose. Harris wrote the scene — the pit, the hose, the command to rub the cream in — but not this sentence. In the 1988 novel ↗ Gumb addresses Catherine as “you”, and the substance is a “skin emollient”, never “lotion”.

Ted Levine delivered the line and Jame Gumb is a fictional character; neither wrote it. The author of a screen line is the screenwriter — here Ted Tally ↗, whose adaptation won the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest credit: the scene is Thomas Harris’s (1988), the sentence is Ted Tally’s, and the verb is rubs — as the film’s transcription ↗ confirms.

context.heading: How a novel’s command became a screen line
lead: The scene is not Ted Tally’s invention. In Thomas Harris’s 1988 novel, Catherine Martin is already in the pit, already washing at gunpoint, already threatened with the hose, and already handed a bottle of what Harris calls a “skin emollient”. Harris even gives Gumb the third-person “it” — but only as a cooing aside to his dog, never aimed at the woman herself. To Catherine he speaks directly: he tells her to wash, or she gets the hose, and then to dry off and rub the cream all over.

What Tally did was move the pronoun. Across his drafts held at the Internet Archive, the second (28 July 1989) and third (25 August 1989) still follow Harris almost exactly, with Gumb barking “Rub it in! Or you’ll get the hose again” and reserving “it” for the dog. By the fourth draft (15 January 1990) the “it” has migrated out of the aside and into the commands themselves. That single grammatical shift — a man refusing to call his captive you — is what made the line unforgettable, and it is Tally’s.
detailsBody: The misquote is not random: put genuinely is in the scene, attached to the basket rather than the skin. Wikiquote’s transcription gives Gumb’s instruction as “Now it places the lotion in the basket”, and moments later, when Catherine baulks, the composure snaps into the shouted “Put the fucking lotion in the basket!” — the loudest and most parodied moment in the sequence.

So a viewer leaves the film having heard lotion paired with both rub and put, and the louder verb wins. Memory keeps the shape of the famous sentence and swaps in the word that was shouted. Notably, Tally’s drafts have Gumb say “bottle” rather than “lotion” in the basket line, and contain no expletive version at all — both appear to be late changes made at or near shooting.
context.pull: Harris supplied the hose and the rubbing. Tally supplied the pronoun — and the pronoun is the horror.
